t: What Truly Satisfies You Is Not the World’s Manna
v: Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
The Jews therefore murmured concerning him, because he said, “I am the bread which came down out of heaven.”
They said, “Isn’t this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, ‘I have come down out of heaven’?”
Therefore Jesus answered them, “Don’t murmur among yourselves.
No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up in the last day.
It is written in the prophets, ‘They will all be taught by God.’ Therefore everyone who hears from the Father and has learned, comes to me.
Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God. He has seen the Father.
Most certainly, I tell you, he who believes in me has eternal life.
I am the bread of life.
Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and they died.
This is the bread which comes down out of heaven, that anyone may eat of it and not die.
I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Yes, the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”
b: Jesus did not say, “I give you bread.” He said, “I am the bread.” What a stunning declaration. The world gives temporary satisfaction; the Lord gives himself. Manna could sustain for a day but could not overcome death; Jesus became the bread, and he brings eternal life.

People often look down on what is familiar. The Jews said, “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?” They saw only his outward identity and missed his heavenly nature. When the focus is on people and their backgrounds, we lose our sensitivity to God’s revelation. The ones who truly come to the Lord are those drawn by the Father and willing to be taught.

Jesus points to a core truth: whoever believes has eternal life. It is not earned by effort, not accumulated by merit, but received by simply trusting him. To eat this bread means to be united with him, letting his life enter into us. When we let Jesus be King and make him the daily bread of our soul, we no longer hold ourselves up, but are nourished by him.
a: Come to the Lord every day to be filled
Don’t seek God only when you need him; treat him as the daily bread of your life.
Don’t look down on the Lord because he is familiar
Ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes, so that you revere and treasure Jesus anew.
Replace arguing with faith
Don’t rely on rational debate; simply believe and simply receive.
q: Is the satisfaction I seek right now temporary manna, or the bread of eternal life?
pr: Lord Jesus, You are the living bread that came down from heaven. Forgive me for so often filling my emptiness with the things of this world and overlooking that You are the true satisfaction. Today I simply come to You, trusting and depending on You, and I let Your life be my strength. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Jesus is my bread of life; I am satisfied by believing in him, and I have eternal life.

t: Don’t Carry It Alone; God Has Prepared Companions for You
v: There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth. “For whom then do I labor and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
b: This passage paints a heartbreaking picture: a person working desperately with no one to share with, accumulating with all his might yet not knowing for whom he lives. Outwardly successful, inwardly lonely. Scripture calls this “vanity,” because from the beginning God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

The way of God’s Kingdom is not fighting alone but walking together. Two working together bear fruit; when one falls, the other lifts him up; when it is cold, there is warmth; in battle, there is someone at your side. This is not weakness; it is a blessing God designed. A spiritual life that depends only on oneself grows weary quickly; with mutual support it can last.

“A threefold cord is not quickly broken” points to a spiritual principle: when God is present in a relationship, it has strength. When a couple centers on God, when a small group has Christ as its head, when co-workers are led by the Holy Spirit, it is not two strands but three. True unity is not held together by human sentiment, but by God reigning in the middle.
a: Step into spiritual relationships
Don’t live your faith as a lone ranger; find companions who can watch over one another.
Learn to support and be supported
Be willing to lift others up, and also willing to accept help when you fall.
Make God the center of your relationships
In family or service, let Jesus be King and be that third strand of the cord.
q: Am I used to carrying it alone, or am I willing to enter the spiritual connections God has prepared for me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for not leaving me in loneliness, but preparing companions to walk with me. Forgive me for the times I acted tough and would not open myself up. Lead me into relationships of unity, where we support one another in love and become a strong cord in You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I no longer walk alone; God is in our midst, and I walk in unity with my spiritual companions.

t: Trials Are Not to Knock You Down, but to Shape You
v: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations,
knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
But let him ask in faith, without any doubting, for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven by the wind and tossed.
For that man shouldn’t think that he will receive anything from the Lord.
He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
b: From the very beginning this passage overturns our instinct: “Count it all joy when you fall into various trials.” The joy is not because of the pain itself, but because we know God is at work in the pain. A trial is like fire, burning away the impurities and leaving pure gold; faith under pressure produces endurance, and endurance leads us into maturity.

God does not want us to stay stuck in merely “holding on”; he wants endurance to have its “perfect work.” That means letting the process run its course, not rushing to escape or giving up casually. When we are willing to keep leaning on the Lord in difficulty, our lives are refined and shaped, and we become perfect and complete. It is not by improving ourselves, but by being polished in God’s hand.

James then points to the key: if you lack wisdom, ask God. What we need most in trials is not ability but a heavenly perspective. But when we ask, we must simply believe, without wavering. A double-minded person is like a wave of the sea with no direction; but one who wholeheartedly leans on the Lord can stand in the storm. Faith is not half God and half self; it is full surrender.
a: Change how you see trials
When facing difficulty today, first ask: What is God shaping in my life?
Practice endurance under pressure
Don’t rush to escape; let God finish the lesson.
Ask God simply for wisdom
Lay down doubt and divided loyalty, and rely on the Lord’s guidance with faith.
q: The trial I face now, do I want to run from it, or am I willing to let God shape me through it?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for not leaving me to get lost in hardship, but for shaping me through trials. Give me heavenly wisdom, so that I do not doubt or waver. Help me still lean wholeheartedly on You in the storm, and let endurance finish its work in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Trials cannot knock me down; God is shaping me, making me perfect and complete.

t: Enemies in the Night, Loving Kindness in the Morning
v: Oh, my Strength, I watch for you, for God is my high tower.
My God will go before me with his loving kindness. God will let me look at my enemies in triumph.
Don’t kill them, or my people may forget. Scatter them by your power, and bring them down, Lord our shield.
For the sin of their mouth, and the words of their lips, let them be caught in their pride, for the curses and lies which they utter.
Consume them in wrath. Consume them, and they will be no more. Let them know that God rules in Jacob, to the ends of the earth. Selah.
At evening let them return. Let them howl like a dog, and go around the city.
They shall wander up and down for food, and wait all night if they aren’t satisfied.
But I will sing of your strength. Yes, I will sing aloud of your loving kindness in the morning. For you have been my high tower, a refuge in the day of my distress.
To you, my strength, I will sing praises. For God is my high tower, the God of my mercy.
b: The setting of this psalm is a time of pursuit and threat. In the night enemies surround the city, with lies, attacks, and unrest. David neither denies the pressure nor pretends to be strong; he honestly cries out to God. But in his crying out he makes a choice: to look up.

He says, “My strength, I will watch for you.” Strength does not come from circumstances, nor from holding ourselves up, but from God. God is the “high tower,” meaning a place from which we see the whole picture; God is the “refuge,” a place to hide in the storm. When a person stands in the high tower, the enemies are still there, but the perspective has changed.

The psalm has a sharp contrast: at night enemies circle like dogs, but in the morning loving kindness greets us. Night represents fear and waiting; morning represents hope and renewal. People who belong to God do not lack dark nights, but even in the dark they decide to sing. This is not a mood swing; it is a declaration of faith—God reigns.

David declares once more at the end: “God is my high tower, the God of my mercy.” The enemies may keep pacing back and forth, but God’s loving kindness is new every morning. This is the rhythm of those who belong to God: looking up at night, singing in the morning.
a: Choose to look up in the dark
Don’t let anxiety take over; first bring your heart up to God’s high tower.
Replace complaining with worship
While the problem is still there, open your mouth to praise God’s loving kindness.
Believe that God reigns
Circumstances shake, but God’s Kingdom does not.
q: When enemies surround me and pressure closes in, is my first reaction panic, or looking up?
pr: Heavenly Father, in my day of distress You are my high tower and my refuge. When night comes and lies surround me, help me still look up to You. Let me sing of Your loving kindness in the morning, and believe that You reign. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The night cannot swallow me; God’s loving kindness will surely greet me in the morning.

t: Treasure in Clay Jars: Glory Revealed in Brokenness
v: For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake,
seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from ourselves.
We are pressed on every side, yet not crushed; perplexed, yet not to despair;
pursued, yet not forsaken; struck down, yet not destroyed;
always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.
For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus may be revealed in our mortal flesh.
So then death works in us, but life in you.
b: Paul is very clear: “We don’t preach ourselves.” True ministry is not exalting people but exalting Christ. Only when we step back can Jesus become the focus. This is the order of life—not I who live, but Christ living in me.

God puts the “treasure” in “clay jars.” Clay jars are fragile, easily broken, and unremarkable; the treasure is precious and glorious. God did not entrust the gospel to perfect people, but to those willing to live in selflessness. When the jar has cracks, the light can shine through; when people admit weakness, it becomes clear that the power is from God.

“Pressed on every side, yet not crushed.” This does not deny pressure; it declares a greater power within. Outside there is persecution, but inside there is the Holy Spirit; outside we are struck down, but inside there is resurrection life. This is the principle of the cross—death works in us, but life works in others.

When we are willing to give up self and let the death of Jesus work in us, his life flows out through us. God’s divine order is not built on human talent but on God’s power; not on human glory but on giving all glory to Jesus.
a: Preach not yourself, but Christ
Examine your motives for serving: is it for the Lord, or for yourself?
Accept that you are a clay jar
Stop pretending to be strong, and let God’s power be made perfect in weakness.
Live out resurrection life under pressure
Even when pressed, believe that God is bringing forth life through me.
q: Am I willing to be a clay jar, so that Jesus’ treasure can be revealed through my life?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for placing the treasure in this clay jar of mine. When I am weak, remind me that the power is not from me but from You. Let the death of Jesus work in me, so that his life is revealed in me and flows to others. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am a clay jar, but the treasure is in me; God’s power is revealed in my weakness.

t: Even in Blessing, Keep Seeking God’s Guidance
v: Abraham was old, and well advanced in age. The LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.
Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had, “Please put your hand under my thigh.
I will make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and the God of the earth, that you shall not take a wife for my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I live.
But you shall go to my country, and to my relatives, and take a wife for my son Isaac.”
The servant took ten of his master’s camels, and departed, having a variety of good things of his master’s with him. He arose, and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.
He made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time that women go out to draw water.
He said, “LORD, the God of my master Abraham, please give me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham.
b: Abraham was one whom “the Lord had blessed in all things,” yet he did not become careless because of it. A truly blessed person does not decide casually just because things go smoothly; at key moments he seeks God all the more carefully. His son’s marriage was not left to circumstances, but placed within God’s covenant.

Here we see a heart for spiritual legacy. Abraham was not concerned only with present comfort; he thought about how God’s promise would continue. Faith is not one generation’s zeal, but generations keeping covenant. Being blessed is not the destination but a responsibility—to let God’s purpose continue to be fulfilled in the next generation.

Even more moving is the servant. He did not say, “I have plenty of experience; I will judge for myself.” When he reached the well, the first thing he did was pray. This is a life of selflessness—using the heart led by the Spirit, not the mind relying on self. Outwardly he prepared ten camels, but inwardly he bowed in humility. True success is not having every resource in place, but having God’s gracious hand with us.
When we still seek God in blessing and still depend on God in responsibility, God makes the way clear. Not by relying on power, not by relying on talent, but by relying on God’s grace.
a: Stay careful in good times
Don’t make decisions on your own just because you are blessed; ask the Lord at every step.
Keep covenant for the next generation
Think about whether my choices let God’s promises continue.
Let prayer be the starting point
Bow down before acting, and seek God’s heart before planning.
q: Now that I am blessed, do I still place important decisions in God’s hands?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for blessing and guiding me all along the way. Keep me from complacency in good times, and from relying on myself in responsibility. Teach me to seek Your heart in everything, so that my life is not only blessed but becomes a vessel that carries Your promises. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Even in blessing I keep seeking God’s guidance, and let the Lord be King in my life.

t: Be a Faithful Steward, Not Your Own King
v: So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants and stewards of God’s mysteries.
Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
You are already filled. You have already become rich. You have come to reign without us. Yes, and I wish that you did reign, that we also might reign with you!
For I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, last of all, like men sentenced to death. For we are made a spectacle to the world, both to angels and men.
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You have honor, but we have dishonor.
Even to this present hour we hunger, thirst, are naked, are beaten, and have no certain dwelling place.
We toil, working with our own hands. When people curse us, we bless. Being persecuted, we endure.
Being defamed, we entreat. We are made as the filth of the world, the dirt wiped off by all, even until now.
b: This passage presents a sharp contrast: on one side, a life that thinks, “I am already full, already rich, already reigning on my own”; on the other, a life willing to stand last and serve faithfully. What looks glorious outwardly may be proud inwardly; what looks lowly outwardly may be honored in God’s eyes.

The values of God’s Kingdom differ from the world’s. The world values position, applause, and success; God looks for faithfulness. When people forget they are stewards, they want to be king; when they remember they are stewards, they are willing to let the Lord be King.

Paul describes the apostles’ condition: hungry, thirsty, toiling, slandered, despised. Yet their response is to bless, endure, and entreat. This is not weakness; it is the life of Christ revealed. True victory is not reigning from a high position, but being faithful in lowliness.
The spiritual danger is not suffering, but “reigning on our own.” Spiritual victory is not holding power, but being faithful.
When we return to our rightful place, letting God be God and human be human, life is no longer about striving for our own glory, but living for the Lord.
a: Examine your motives
Do I serve for my own glory, or to be faithful to what God has entrusted to me?
Be faithful in small things
What God values is not the size of the position, but a faithful and steady heart.
Respond to hurt the way Christ does
When misunderstood, still bless; when pressured, still endure; let Jesus be King.
q: Am I building a throne for myself, or faithfully managing all that God has entrusted to me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for choosing me to be a servant of Christ and a steward of Your mysteries. Forgive me for wanting to be my own king and for seeking people’s praise and position. Give me a faithful and humble heart, willing to stand last, and let Jesus reign in my life. May I not strive for my own glory all my life, but be faithful to You to the end. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am a faithful steward of God’s mysteries; I will not be my own king, and I let Jesus reign in my life.

t: Rise Up from Failure and Win Again
v: The LORD said to Joshua, “Don’t be afraid, and don’t be dismayed. Take all the warriors with you, and arise, go up to Ai. Behold, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, with his people, his city, and his land.
The LORD said to Joshua, “Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand.” Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.
The ambush arose quickly out of their place, and they ran as soon as he had stretched out his hand and entered into the city and took it. They hurried and set the city on fire.

When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the field, in the wilderness in which they pursued them, and they had all fallen by the edge of the sword until they were consumed, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it with the edge of the sword.
For Joshua didn’t draw back his hand, with which he stretched out the javelin, until he had utterly destroyed all the inhabitants of Ai.
Israel took for themselves only the livestock and the goods of that city, according to the LORD’s word which he commanded Joshua.
b: Ai was once a mark of failure. In the previous battle, Israel was defeated because of sin, and their hearts melted like water. But God did not let failure be the end. He said to Joshua, “Don’t be afraid, neither be dismayed.” True revival begins with God’s voice, not with human self-blame.

God did more than comfort; he gave a strategy. This time they did not charge ahead in the flesh, but set an ambush as God instructed. Victory does not come from human impulse but from obedience. When Joshua stretched out his javelin, it was an act of faith—outwardly a hand stretched out, inwardly trust in God’s word.

And Joshua did not lower his hand halfway, but kept it out until the victory was complete. This reminds us: obedience cannot be only half done, and faith cannot last only a moment. Those who rise up from failure must keep depending on God until his purpose is accomplished.

This passage also shows us that when people return to God’s order, God restores blessing. What was lost through sin is regained through repentance and obedience. The focus is not Ai, but whether God is King among us.
a: Don’t let failure define you
Having fallen does not mean God’s plan is over. Listen to God’s voice and rise again.
Fight God’s way
Don’t act on impulsive emotion; receive God’s strategy in prayer.
Obey to the end
Don’t quit halfway; let your faith hold firm to the finish.
q: Am I still stuck in past failures, or am I willing to listen to God’s word and rise again?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for not giving up on me when I failed. Give me the courage to rise again, and the faith to obey to the end. Let me not rely on my own strength, but depend completely on Your guidance until victory comes. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am not held captive by failure; I rise again through the Lord, until I fully win.

t: For Whom Are You Storing Up Your Life?
v: One of the multitude said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?”
He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”
He spoke a parable to them, saying, “The ground of a certain rich man produced abundantly.
He reasoned within himself, saying, ‘What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?’
He said, ‘This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.
I will tell my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.”’
“But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’
So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
b: This conversation begins with dividing an inheritance, but it exposes a deeper problem—greed in the heart. Jesus did not help him divide the estate; instead he pointed out that the real danger is not an unequal inheritance but a life bound by covetousness.

The rich man’s problem was not that he had wealth, but that he lived “only for himself.” His thoughts were full of “my crops,” “my barns,” “my grain,” “my soul.” His whole world revolved around himself. This is the old self’s self-centeredness—centered on self, wanting to be king.

But God called him a “foolish one.” He calculated this life carefully yet neglected eternity; he arranged his wealth but did not prepare his soul. Life does not consist in the abundance of possessions but in one’s relationship with God. True riches are not the numbers in a bank, but abundance before God.

When we let Jesus be King, possessions are no longer master but become tools; life is no longer about storing up for ourselves but offering ourselves for God’s Kingdom. This is the turn from “storing up treasure for ourselves” to being “rich toward God.”
a: Examine your motives
Do I work hard for security, or for the glory of God?
Practice generosity and sharing
Let what God has given become a channel of blessing to others.
Invest in eternity
Put your time, energy, and resources into the values of God.
q: If God required my soul tonight, would I already be rich toward him?
pr: Heavenly Father, shine on the hidden greed in my heart, so that I no longer build bigger barns for myself, but let Jesus be King in my life. Help me live a life of selflessness, placing everything in Your hands, and become an eternal blessing. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not store up treasure for myself; I am rich toward God, and I let Jesus be the King of my life.

t: Rich Toward God
v: One of the multitude said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or an arbitrator over you?”
He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”
He spoke a parable to them, saying, “The ground of a certain rich man produced abundantly.
He reasoned within himself, saying, ‘What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?’
He said, ‘This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.
I will tell my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.”’
“But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’
So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
b: This passage begins with a family dispute over an inheritance, but it reveals a deeper problem—greed. The man asked Jesus to settle the division, which looked like a pursuit of fairness but actually exposed an attachment in his heart. The Lord did not divide the property for him; instead he reminded the crowd: “A man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.” What truly determines the worth of a life is not how much we own, but whom our heart turns to.

The rich man’s land was abundant, which was a grace, but his heart held only “my”—my crops, my barns, my goods. He planned his future for himself, yet did not include God in that future. This is the old self’s self-centeredness: security found in accumulation, protection found in wealth, while eternity is ignored.

God called him a “foolish one,” because he counted only the years on earth and did not prepare treasure in heaven. That night his soul was taken, and everything came to nothing. The Lord concluded: “So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.” True riches mean letting Jesus be King and living abundantly before God, not merely possessing abundance on earth.
a: Examine what you rely on
Is my sense of security built on possessions, or in God?
Invest in eternity
Use your time and resources for the Kingdom of God and for loving others.
Let Jesus reign
Be a faithful steward, not one who stores up treasure for himself.
q: Am I pursuing earthly abundance, or being rich before God?
pr: Heavenly Father, shine on my heart so that I am not ruled by greed. Teach me that life does not consist in how much I own, but in whether I walk with You. Help me become truly rich before God, and let Jesus be King in my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: My life does not rely on possessions for security; I am rich before God, and I let Jesus reign in my heart.

t: In the Wilderness, God Never Left
v: yet you in your manifold mercies didn’t forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud didn’t depart from over them by day, to lead them in the way; neither did the pillar of fire by night, to show them light, and the way in which they should go.
You gave also your good Spirit to instruct them, and didn’t withhold your manna from their mouth, and gave them water for their thirst.
“Yes, forty years you sustained them in the wilderness. They lacked nothing. Their clothes didn’t grow old, and their feet didn’t swell.
b: This passage looks back on Israel’s forty years in the wilderness and stresses one thing: God never left them. The wilderness was not a place where God abandoned them, but a place where he showed his mercy. The pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire stayed with them day and night, showing God’s constant presence and guidance. Even when the people were weak, complaining, and even rebellious, God still kept his covenant and showed his steadfast love.

God did not only guide them in direction; he also provided for their daily lives. He gave his good Spirit to teach them so they could understand the way, he gave manna for food, and he gave water for their thirst. The wilderness may be barren, but it was not a place of lack, because God himself was their provider. Spiritual growth often happens not in comfort but in dependence.

For forty years they “lacked nothing.” Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell. This was supernatural protection. The wilderness did not change God’s faithfulness; it only revealed it. When circumstances are hard, we easily doubt, but the truth is this: God sustains us in the wilderness so that we learn to depend on him alone.
a: See God’s presence in hardship
Don’t look only at your circumstances; watch for God’s pillar of cloud and fire.
Learn to receive God’s instruction
Let the Holy Spirit shape your life in the wilderness.
Trust God’s provision
Even when the road is long, God will make sure you lack nothing.
q: Do I believe that even in the wilderness, God still shows great mercy and has never left me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for being with me in the wilderness of my life. When I am weak, You do not forsake me; when I am lost, You still guide me. Help me to learn to depend on You in hardship, and to trust Your provision and protection. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Whatever wilderness I walk through, God is with me, and I lack nothing.

t: Revived by God’s Word in Affliction
v: Remember your word to your servant, because you gave me hope.
This is my comfort in my affliction, for your word has revived me.
The arrogant mock me excessively, but I don’t swerve from your law.
I remember your ordinances of old, LORD, and have comforted myself.
Indignation has taken hold on me, because of the wicked who forsake your law.
Your statutes have been my songs in the house where I live.
I have remembered your name, LORD, in the night, and I obey your law.
This is my way, that I keep your precepts.
b: This passage shows us a life in affliction that did not collapse but was instead “revived” by God’s word. The psalmist doesn’t deny his difficulties; he admits he is mocked and surrounded by pressure. Yet his hope is not that circumstances will change, but that God’s promise will stand. When he cries, “Remember the word… because you have made me hope,” he is holding on to God’s word. God’s word is not mere theory; it is a power that makes people live again.

The psalmist says, “Your word has revived me.” In affliction, what truly comforts us is not human reassurance but God’s ordinances from of old. When the arrogant mock him, he does not swerve from the law; when the wicked forsake the truth, he becomes even more resolute. His foundation is not in what people think, but in God’s eternal word. This is trusting the Lord with the heart, rather than calculating circumstances with the mind.

Even more precious, in his pilgrim life he makes God’s statutes his songs, and in the night he remembers God’s name. This is not forced; it is a response of love. Obedience is not a burden but the natural overflow of life. “This is my way, because I keep your precepts.” When God’s word becomes our joy, we are no longer swallowed up by affliction, but find victory in the midst of it.
a: Hold on to God’s promises in hardship
Don’t look only at circumstances; let God’s word be your hope.
Don’t drift from the truth because of others’ voices
Keep holding to God’s word under pressure.
Let God’s word become your song
Think on it by day and remember him at night, so your life is filled with truth.
q: In affliction, am I driven by my circumstances, or revived by God’s word?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for giving precious promises that give me hope in affliction. Help me not to be shaken by the voices of others, and let Your word be my comfort and strength. Help me to remember You day and night, and to faithfully keep Your precepts even in hard times. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: God’s word revives me; in affliction I still have hope, and I will not turn from the Lord’s truth.

t: Seek Him While He May Be Found
v: Seek the LORD while he may be found. Call on him while he is near.
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts. Let him return to the LORD, and he will have mercy on him, to our God, for he will freely pardon.
“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,” says the LORD.
“For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.
For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater;
so is my word that goes out of my mouth: it will not return to me void, but it will accomplish that which I please, and it will prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
For you shall go out with joy, and be led out with peace. The mountains and the hills will break out before you into singing; and all the trees of the fields will clap their hands.
Instead of the thorn the cypress tree will come up; and instead of the brier the myrtle tree will come up. It will make a name for the LORD, for an everlasting sign that will not be cut off.”
b: This passage is a gentle yet urgent call: “Seek Yahweh while he may be found.” The door of God’s grace is open and forgiveness is already prepared; people only need to be willing to return. To forsake our own ways and put away our own thoughts is to let go of the direction of the old self-centered life and come back to God’s way. He is not a stingy God, but one who “will abundantly pardon.”

God goes on to remind us that his thoughts are higher than ours. Often we are confused because we read heavenly plans through earthly eyes. When we humbly admit that God’s ways are higher than ours, we move from complaining to trusting. Change your mindset and your life changes; when we turn from a human point of view to God’s point of view, our life enters a new order.

Finally, God uses rain and snow as an illustration: his word never returns empty. Just as rain waters the ground and makes it sprout and bear fruit, God’s word will accomplish his purpose. When we return, we go out with joy and are led in peace; desolate land will grow cypress, and thorny ground will grow myrtle. This is the change from curse to blessing, from the old life to the new life.
a: Seize the moment to return
Don’t delay; respond to his call while God is near.
Lay down your own thoughts
Learn to trust God’s plans and ways, which are higher than everything.
Let God’s word be fulfilled in your life
Read, reflect, and practice every day, so that your life bears fruit.
q: Am I still clinging to my own way, or am I willing to turn to God’s higher way?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for abundantly pardoning and opening the door of grace to me. Help me to forsake my own ways and turn to Yours. Help me believe that Your word will surely be fulfilled, and let me walk forward in You with joy and peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I turn to the Lord, God’s word will be fulfilled in my life, and I walk forward with joy and peace.

t: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus and Run Without Losing Heart
v: Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us,
looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
For consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don’t grow weary, fainting in your souls.
b: This passage pictures the spiritual life as a race. We do not run alone; before us is a cloud of witnesses from every age, reminding us that the path of faith is real and can be walked. But to run well we must “lay aside every weight and the sin that entangles.” Often the road is not too hard; we are simply carrying too much. If we do not put down pride, bitterness, and self-centeredness, our steps will be slowed.

Then comes the key: “looking to Jesus.” Not at ourselves, and not at others, but fixing our eyes on the author and perfecter of faith. Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him. He was not defined by shame, because he saw eternal glory. When our focus is on Jesus, suffering is no longer the end but the road to victory.

Finally, the passage tells us to “consider” him. Considering is not a passing thought but deep reflection. When we reflect on how the Lord endured opposition and persecution, we won’t grow weary or lose heart. Spiritual fatigue mostly comes from focusing on circumstances; spiritual strength comes from focusing on Christ. When Jesus becomes the focus of everything, our lives can keep moving forward in perseverance.
a: Lay down your burdens
Examine your heart for sin or burdens that slow you down, and give them to the Lord.
Fix your eyes on Jesus
Reflect on the Lord’s example each day and let him be your source of strength.
Keep going in perseverance
Don’t stop because of a moment’s difficulty; keep going until you finish the race.
q: Right now, is my focus as I run my circumstances, or Jesus?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You that I do not run the race of faith alone. Help me lay down my burdens and put aside the sin that entangles, and fix my eyes on Jesus. When I grow weary, remind me to consider the Lord’s perseverance and victory, so that I do not lose heart and can finish the race. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I lay down my burdens and fix my eyes on Jesus; I run with perseverance, without growing weary or losing heart.

t: Stand Still and See God’s Salvation
v: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to the children of Israel, that they turn back and encamp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, before Baal Zephon. You shall encamp opposite it by the sea.
Pharaoh will say of the children of Israel, ‘They are entangled in the land. The wilderness has shut them in.’
I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and he will follow after them; and I will get honor over Pharaoh, and over all his armies; and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD.” They did so.
The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the children of Israel; for the children of Israel went out with a high hand.
When Pharaoh came near, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them; and they were very afraid. The children of Israel cried out to the LORD.
They said to Moses, “Because there were no graves in Egypt, have you taken us away to die in the wilderness? Why have you treated us this way, to bring us out of Egypt?

Isn’t this the word that we spoke to you in Egypt, saying, ‘Leave us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians’? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.”
Moses said to the people, “Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today; for you will never again see the Egyptians whom you have seen today.
The LORD will fight for you, and you shall be still.”
b: This passage is a picture full of tension: the Red Sea in front, the pursuing army behind. What is more remarkable is that this “impossible situation” was no accident; God himself arranged it. God told them to turn back and camp there, and even foretold that Pharaoh would pursue them. In other words, sometimes God allows difficulty so that his glory may be displayed. They seemed trapped, but it was all within God’s plan.

When the people saw the Egyptian army approaching, they were afraid, they complained, and they regretted leaving. They would rather go back to being slaves than face the unknown of the wilderness. This is the habit of the old life: fearing freedom and longing for bondage. When we look at circumstances with our natural eyes, we lose faith; when we remember only the pain of the past and forget God’s grace, we easily lose heart.

Moses, however, spoke the key words: “Don’t be afraid. Stand still!” The first step of victory is not running but standing still; not struggling but being quiet. For “Yahweh will fight for you.” True faith is letting God be King and returning to our rightful place. When we stop fighting in our own strength and depend wholly on the Lord, the Red Sea becomes a road.
a: Trust God’s plan in a desperate situation
Don’t rush to judge your circumstances; God may be preparing a greater victory.
Choose to stand still in the face of fear
Stop complaining and panicking, and entrust your heart to the Lord.
Learn to let God fight
Don’t struggle on your own; rely on God’s power alone.
q: When I face a Red Sea with an army behind me, do I respond with fear and complaint, or do I stand still and see God’s salvation?
pr: Heavenly Father, when I face a situation that seems to have no way out, help me not to fear or complain. Teach me to stand still and look to what You are doing. Let me believe that You will fight for me, and that my difficulty will become a place that testifies to Your glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am not afraid; I stand still and look to God. The Lord will fight for me, and I will see his salvation.

t: Living as Foreigners, Walking Like Christ
v: Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul,
having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.
Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme,
or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well.
For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.
Live as free people, yet not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.
Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.
Servants, be in subjection to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the wicked.
For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience toward God.
For what glory is it if, when you sin, you patiently endure beating? But if when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God.
For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps,
b: This passage reminds us of an identity: we are foreigners and pilgrims. Since we are not permanent residents of this world, we should not be pulled along by its desires. Fleshly lusts wage war against the soul, and the real battlefield is not outside but within. If we are not watchful, freedom can easily become license, and grace an excuse.

Peter goes on to teach that among the Gentiles we should live with good conduct. A Christian’s witness is not only preaching but daily life. Even when slandered and misunderstood, we still respond with good deeds. When people see good works, they will in the end give glory to God. This is the principle of God’s Kingdom: we silence people not by arguing but by doing good.

Finally, Peter turns the focus to Christ. If we endure suffering for doing good, it is commendable before God. Christ suffered for us and left us an example. He did not defend himself but submitted to the end. To follow in his steps is to remain faithful when treated unfairly and keep a clear conscience under pressure. This is not weakness but heavenly strength.
a: Recognize your identity as a pilgrim
Don’t let desires rule your life; remember that you belong to God’s Kingdom.
Witness to the Lord through good deeds
Keep doing good even when misunderstood, and give the glory to God.
Follow in Christ’s steps
Endure in suffering and keep a conscience clear before God.
q: When I suffer unfairly, do I complain and argue, or do I follow in Christ’s steps?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for calling me to live as a pilgrim in this world yet belong to Your Kingdom. Help me abstain from fleshly desires and live with good conduct before the world. When I face unfair treatment, give me strength to endure and follow in Christ’s steps, so that the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am a pilgrim in this world; I abstain from fleshly desires and follow in Christ’s steps, staying faithful in suffering.

t: Remember Him Until He Comes
v: For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread.
When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”
In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
b: This passage takes us back to that night, the night the Lord was betrayed. Darkness was about to fall and the cross was just ahead, yet Jesus took the bread and the cup and instituted the Lord’s Supper. He did not run from suffering but gave himself up willingly. The bread symbolizes his body given for us, and the cup symbolizes the new covenant sealed with his blood. This is not a religious ritual but the heart of redemption.

The Lord said, “Do this in memory of me.” To remember is not merely to recall, but to bring his self-giving into our life today. Every time we eat the bread and drink the cup, we are reminded that our life was bought with his precious blood. If so, we no longer live for ourselves, but let Jesus be King. This is the move from the law of the old covenant into the grace of the new covenant.

“Until he comes.” The Lord’s Supper does not only look back; it also points forward. The Lord’s death has accomplished salvation, and his return will complete the glory. Each time we receive the bread and cup, we proclaim that the cross is real, the resurrection is real, and our hope is real. We live between the “already” and the “not yet,” waiting for that day with thankful hearts.
a: Reflect often on the cross
Let Christ’s self-giving be the foundation of each day’s life.
Live in new covenant grace
Stop living for yourself and let Jesus reign in your heart.
Wait for the Lord’s return with hope
Live faithfully in this age until the Lord comes again.
q: When I receive the bread and cup, do I sincerely remember the Lord’s self-giving and live out the life that belongs to him?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus to give his body and shed his blood for me and establish the new covenant. Help me, each time I remember the Lord, not to do it as a mere form but as a renewal of life. Let me reflect often on the cross and live in thankfulness and hope until the Lord comes again. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I remember the Lord’s self-giving, I live in new covenant grace, and I wait for his return with hope.

t: Let Love Be the Sign
v: Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.
By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him.
In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.
b: This passage puts love at the very center of faith. Love is not a human emotion but the very nature that comes from God. “God is love.” Without love, even if we claim to know God, we still do not understand him. A truly born-again person will inevitably show love in life, because love is the mark of a life that belongs to God.

God’s love is not an abstract idea but concrete action: he sent his only Son to be the atoning sacrifice for our sins. This is the love of the cross, a love that takes the initiative and gives itself up. It was not that we loved God first, but that he loved us first. When we understand this grace, our hearts are renewed; we are no longer centered on ourselves, but compelled by love to love others.

John says, “If we love one another, God remains in us.” Though no one has seen God, we can see his presence in our love for one another. When the church, the family, and the fellowship live out love for one another, God’s glory is revealed among them. Love is not weakness but heavenly power; it is not a slogan but the work God perfects within us.
a: Start from being loved
Reflect often that God loved you first, and let your heart be softened.
Live out love in action
Take the initiative to forgive, bear with others, and give in your relationships.
Let God’s love be perfected in you
Reject coldness and self-centeredness, and let Jesus be King.
q: Does my life let people see God’s love, or does my love stay only in words?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me first and sending Jesus to be the atoning sacrifice for my sins. Fill my heart with Your love, so that I not only receive love but also live it out. Let Your presence be revealed through our love for one another, so that the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: God is love; I am loved by him and I live out his love, so that God remains in me.

t: Where Is Your Treasure?
v: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.

Therefore, when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.
But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does,
so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.
“Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal;
but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal;
for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
b: This passage uncovers a core question: motive. The Lord Jesus is not against doing good; he reminds us to ask for whom we do it. If it is to gain the glory of people, we have already received their applause but lost our Father’s reward. Outwardly we may look devout while inwardly still living a self-centered life. Truly godly good deeds are done in secret, so that God receives the glory and not ourselves.

Next, the Lord turns the focus to treasure. Earthly wealth rusts, is lost, and can be stolen, but treasure in heaven never disappears. Storing up treasure in heaven is not only about giving money; it is investing our lives in eternal values: loving others, doing good, and obeying God. When Jesus is King, we no longer store up for ourselves, but live for God’s Kingdom.

The last sentence goes straight to the heart: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Treasure does not mean only money, but whatever you care about most. If your heart is drawn to the world, you will live for the earth; if your heart belongs to God, you will live for heaven. Change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and the direction of your investment changes.
a: Examine your motives for doing good
Is today’s giving to win people’s praise, or to please my Father?
Invest in eternity
Put your time and resources into the Kingdom of God, not only into earthly gain.
Guard your heart
Ask yourself often: what do I care about most?
q: Where does my heart rest right now? Does my treasure point to earth, or to heaven?
pr: Heavenly Father, cleanse my motives, so that I do good not to win people’s glory but to please You. Help me store up treasure in heaven and turn my heart to You. Let Jesus be King in my life, so that all glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: My treasure is in heaven, my heart belongs to God, and I do good only for my Father’s glory.

t: The Stone Has Been Rolled Away
v: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, that they might come and anoint him.
Very early on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb when the sun had risen.
They were saying among themselves, “Who will roll away the stone from the door of the tomb for us?”
for it was very big. Looking up, they saw that the stone was rolled back.
Entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe; and they were amazed.
He said to them, “Don’t be amazed. You seek Jesus, the Nazarene, who has been crucified. He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him!
But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he said to you.’”
They went out, and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had come on them. They said nothing to anyone; for they were afraid.
b: This passage records the stunning moment of resurrection morning. The women came to the tomb with spices, their hearts full of sorrow and confusion. Their biggest question was, “Who will roll away the stone for us?” This is the human point of view: seeing the difficulty, seeing the obstacle, seeing the impossible. But when they looked up, the stone had already been rolled away. God had been at work before they arrived.

The angel declared, “He has risen. He is not here.” These words overturned history and overturned lives. The cross is not the end, and the tomb is not the final chapter. Jesus has conquered death and become the foundation of our faith. When our focus is on Jesus and not on the stone, we can move from fear into hope.

The women were trembling and astonished, because the resurrection goes beyond human understanding. The message of the resurrection first brings a shock, and then brings a mission: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter.” Even Peter, who had fallen, was called by name. The resurrection brings not only power but also restoration. When we have met the risen Lord, we no longer stay before the tomb, but are sent out toward the future.
a: Look up at what God has done
Don’t just stare at the stone; believe God is already working ahead of you.
Keep your focus on the risen Lord
Difficulty is not the end; Jesus has already won.
Respond to the mission of the resurrection
Boldly share the grace you have experienced.
q: Am I still standing grieving before the tomb, or do I believe the stone has been rolled away?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for raising Jesus from the dead and giving me eternal hope. When I face the stones in my life, help me look up to You and believe You have already opened the way for me. Let the power of the resurrection work in my life, so that I no longer fear but go forward boldly. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The stone has been rolled away and Jesus has risen; I do not fear, and I go forward with hope.

t: When People Make Idols, God’s Tablets Are Shattered
v: Moses turned, and went down from the mountain, with the two tablets of the covenant in his hand; tablets that were written on both their sides. They were written on one side and on the other.
The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.
When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, “There is the noise of war in the camp.”
He said, “It isn’t the voice of those who shout for victory. It is not the voice of those who cry for being overcome; but the noise of those who sing that I hear.”
As soon as he came near to the camp, he saw the calf and the dancing. Then Moses’ anger grew hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands, and broke them beneath the mountain.
He took the calf which they had made, and burned it with fire, ground it to powder, and scattered it on the water, and made the children of Israel drink it.
Moses said to Aaron, “What did these people do to you, that you have brought a great sin on them?”
Aaron said, “Don’t let the anger of my lord grow hot. You know the people, that they are set on evil.
For they said to me, ‘Make us gods, which shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.’
I said to them, ‘Whoever has any gold, let them take it off.’ So they gave it to me; and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf.”
b: This passage presents a great contrast: on the mountain, tablets written by God’s own hand; at the foot of the mountain, a golden calf made by human hands. The tablets represent God’s heart and covenant; the calf represents human impatience and unbelief. When the people could not wait, they used their own way to “make a god they could see.” This is precisely the old self-centered life: unwilling to wait on God, only wanting to control the direction.

Moses heard singing, but it was not the cheer of victory; it was the revelry of people who had turned aside. The form of worship was there, but God was not. When people think they are worshiping, they may actually be exalting themselves. An idol does not have to be a golden calf; it can be security, power, money, or reputation. When the heart leaves God, no amount of excitement can keep it from being empty.

Even more sobering is Aaron’s excuse: “I threw it into the fire, and this calf came out.” After sinning, people often shift the blame, as if the idol appeared by itself. In truth, idols are never accidents; they are the choice of the human heart. When we leave our rightful place and grasp an authority that does not belong to us, we unknowingly create “a god of our own.”

True repentance is returning to God’s covenant; true renewal is letting God write on our hearts again. Don’t let a moment’s anxiety bring lasting brokenness. Let Jesus be King, and idols will be crushed on their own.
a: Examine the idols in your heart
Today, am I replacing God’s leading with my own way?
Learn to wait on God
Keep trusting in uncertainty, and don’t rush to take control yourself.
Face responsibility honestly
Don’t shift blame or rationalize; let God shine his light and renew you.
q: In my anxiety, am I making my own “golden calf”?
pr: Heavenly Father, shine Your light on the hidden idols in my heart. Forgive me for the times I left Your leading in my anxiety and tried to take Your place with my own way. Help me return to Your covenant, let Your word be written on my heart, and worship You alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will not make idols; I return to God’s covenant, and I let Jesus be King in my heart.

t: Doers of the Word Find True Freedom
v: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
b: This passage points straight at a spiritual crisis: hearing a lot and doing little. James says that to hear the word without doing it is to “delude your own selves.” To delude is not to be deceived by others, but to think we are spiritual while our lives have not changed. Knowledge without practice only becomes self-comfort.

James uses the picture of a mirror. God’s word is like a mirror that shows us our true face. The problem is not in seeing, but in whether we respond. If we see and then turn away and forget, our lives are not renewed. Often we are moved while listening to a message, but leave and return to how we were; this is “hearing and forgetting.”

The truly blessed person is the one who looks intently and “continues.” God’s law is not a chain but sets people free. When we live out the truth, our lives are actually set free. Doing the word is not a burden but the road into freedom and blessing. Change your mindset and your life changes; when life changes, we are blessed in what we do.
a: Put it into practice as soon as you hear
After every message, ask yourself: how will I live this out?
Let truth keep shining on you
Don’t be enlightened only at gatherings; practice it in everyday life too.
Pursue true freedom
Obey God’s word and experience change from the inside out.
q: Am I moved while listening to the word, or changed by doing it?
pr: Heavenly Father, help me not only to hear Your word but to live it out. Shine on the places in my life that need to change, so that I no longer deceive myself. Let me find freedom in obedience and blessing in practice. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am not only a hearer of the word but a doer; I find freedom in obedience and blessing in practice.

t: A Son’s Identity, a Servant’s Attitude
v: When they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma coins came to Peter, and said, “Doesn’t your teacher pay the didrachma?”

He said, “Yes.” When he came into the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive toll or tribute? From their children, or from strangers?”
Peter said to him, “From strangers.” Jesus said to him, “Therefore the children are exempt.

But, lest we cause them to stumble, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take up the first fish that comes up. When you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater coin. Take that, and give it to them for me and you.”
b: This passage reveals a spiritual truth: the balance between identity and attitude. Jesus asked Peter, “From whom do kings collect taxes?” The answer was: from strangers, not from their own children. This means that Jesus, as the Son of God, could have been exempt from the tax. He is not bound by the system, because he is the King’s Son. This reminds us that believers in Christ have the identity of sons, not slaves and not strangers.

Yet Jesus chose to pay the tax. Not because he lacked the right, but because he did not want to be a stumbling block. “Lest we cause them to stumble.” This is the mark of a mature life: having authority but not abusing it, having freedom but being willing to lay it down. A truly godly person does not fight for rights but lives in humility.

Even more wonderful, Jesus told Peter to go fishing and find the coin in the fish’s mouth. This shows God’s provision. When we obey God’s leading, even in seemingly ordinary actions, we can experience supernatural preparation. A son’s identity together with a servant’s heart lives out a life that glorifies God.
a: Affirm your identity
I am God’s child, not an outsider who stands condemned.
Lay down your rights
Learn humility in freedom, and don’t let anyone stumble because of me.
Trust his provision
Obey God’s leading and experience his wonderful preparation.
q: Do I stress only my own rights while neglecting love and humility?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for making me Your child in Christ. Help me not to abuse my freedom but to serve others with a humble heart. Teach me to experience Your provision through obedience, so that my life glorifies You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I have a son’s identity and a servant’s attitude; in obedience I experience God’s provision.

t: A Life of Faith, Love, and Hope
v: We always give thanks to God for all of you, mentioning you in our prayers,
remembering without ceasing your work of faith and labor of love and perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before our God and Father.
We know, brothers loved by God, that you are chosen,
and that our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit and with much assurance. You know what kind of men we showed ourselves to be among you for your sake.
You became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit,
so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia.
b: This passage describes a mature church: faith, love, and hope all moving together. Faith is not a slogan but a “work”; love is not a feeling but a “labor”; hope is not fantasy but “perseverance” in difficulty. A life that truly belongs to God will surely bear visible fruit.

Paul says their gospel came not in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit. This reminds us that faith is not an accumulation of knowledge but the result of the Holy Spirit working in the heart. When truth enters a life, it brings change. Only when life is renewed first can relationships and ministry be healthy. This is the spiritual order from the inside out.

Even more precious, they had joy “in much affliction.” This joy did not come from circumstances but was given by the Holy Spirit. When a church imitates the Lord in suffering, it becomes an example to others. An example is not self-promotion but the natural overflow of life. When faith, love, and hope are all present together, a community lives out a life that glorifies God.
a: Let faith take action
Today, have I turned my faith into concrete service?
Bear labor with love
Be willing to pay a price in relationships, rather than seeking only comfort.
Persevere in hope
Whatever the circumstances, hold on to the hope of the Lord’s return.
q: Does my life show faith, love, and hope together?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for choosing me, so that in Christ I have faith, love, and hope. Let my faith become action, let my love be willing to labor, and let my hope persevere in hardship. Make me an example to others, to the glory of Your name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I live out the work of faith, the labor of love, and the perseverance of hope, and I become an example that glorifies God.

t: Do Not Fear, I Will Help You
v: “But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham my friend,
you whom I have taken hold of from the ends of the earth, and called from its corners, and said to you, ‘You are my servant. I have chosen you and have not cast you away.’
Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.
Behold, all those who are incensed against you will be disappointed and confounded. Those who strive with you will be like nothing, and shall perish.
You will seek them, and won’t find them, even those who contend with you. Those who war against you will be as nothing, as a nonexistent thing.
For I, the LORD your God, will hold your right hand, saying to you, ‘Don’t be afraid. I will help you.’
Don’t be afraid, you worm Jacob, and you men of Israel. I will help you,” says the LORD. “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.
b: This passage is filled with God’s gentle yet firm voice: “Do not fear.” First he reminds his people of their identity: “whom I have chosen,” “my servant,” “I have not cast you away.” In the midst of upheaval and threats, God first establishes the relationship. It is not because we are strong, but because he has chosen us. When identity is settled, fear begins to loosen its grip.

God does not only say “Do not fear”; he gives the reason: “For I am with you.” He promises to strengthen, help, and uphold. He is not watching from afar but “holds your right hand.” The right hand symbolizes strength and action, which means God personally takes us by the hand and leads us forward. When our focus is on God and not on circumstances, our hearts move from dismay to peace.

God even calls his people “you worm Jacob.” This is not an insult but a contrast. Human weakness stands in sharp contrast with God’s power. Precisely because we are small, he is shown to be great. With the Redeemer on our side, even the greatest enemy is as nothing. Humility leads us to depend, and dependence leads us to victory.
a: Confirm your identity
I am chosen by God, loved, and never cast away.
Hold on to promises in fear
Replace the dismay in your heart with God’s word.
Depend humbly on the Redeemer
Admit your weakness and let God be your strength.
q: When fear comes, do I still believe God is holding my right hand?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for choosing me and not casting me away. When I am weak and afraid, hold my right hand and let me know You are with me. Let me be strengthened in dependence and empowered in humility. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: God is with me and I fear no more; he holds my right hand and leads me forward to victory.

t: Earnestly Seeking Him in a Dry Land
v: God, you are my God. I will earnestly seek you. My soul thirsts for you. My flesh longs for you, in a dry and weary land, where there is no water.
So I have seen you in the sanctuary, watching your power and your glory.
Because your loving kindness is better than life, my lips shall praise you.
So I will bless you while I live. I will lift up my hands in your name.
My soul shall be satisfied as with the richest food. My mouth shall praise you with joyful lips,
For you have been my help. I will rejoice in the shadow of your wings.
My soul stays close to you. Your right hand holds me up.
But those who seek my soul to destroy it shall go into the lower parts of the earth.
They shall be given over to the power of the sword. They shall be jackal food.
But the king shall rejoice in God. Everyone who swears by him will praise him, for the mouth of those who speak lies shall be silenced.
b: This psalm was written in the wilderness. The surroundings were dry, but David’s heart was full of longing. He did not drift from God because of hard circumstances; he sought him all the more earnestly. True hunger is not for lack of water, but for lack of God. When the world cannot satisfy, the heart is awakened instead. The wilderness became the place where his spiritual life ran deepest.

David says, “Your loving kindness is better than life.” This is a profound declaration. However precious life is, it is not better than God’s love. When people come to know God’s loving kindness, they can still praise him in hardship. Praise is not because things are going well, but because of who God is. Worship turns dryness into fruitfulness and weariness into satisfaction.

“My soul stays close to you. Your right hand holds me up.” This is a two-way picture: a person holding on to God, and God holding up that person. When we choose to follow closely, God’s right hand supports us. Even if enemies exist, the final outcome still belongs to God. The wilderness is not the end; walking with God is the way.
a: Seek God in dryness
Don’t wait for circumstances to improve before drawing near to God.
Respond to hardship with praise
Let God’s loving kindness be the source of your joy.
Follow the Lord closely
Hold on to God’s promises even in uncertainty.
q: Do I long for God in dry times, or do I forget him in comfort?
pr: Heavenly Father, in the wilderness of my life, make me long for You more deeply. Let me see Your power and glory, and let Your loving kindness be my greatest satisfaction. Help me follow You closely and believe that Your right hand is holding me up. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: In the dry land I still long for God; his loving kindness is better than life, and his right hand holds me up as I go forward.

t: Tear Your Heart and Return to Him
v: “Yet even now,” says the LORD, “turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.”
Tear your heart and not your garments, and turn to the LORD, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity.
Who knows? He may turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, even a meal offering and a drink offering to the LORD, your God.
Blow the trumpet in Zion! Sanctify a fast. Call a solemn assembly.
Gather the people. Sanctify the assembly. Assemble the elders. Gather the children, and those who nurse from breasts. Let the bridegroom go out of his room, and the bride out of her chamber.

Let the priests, the ministers of the LORD, weep between the porch and the altar, and let them say, “Spare your people, LORD, and don’t give your heritage to reproach, that the nations should rule over them. Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’”
Then the LORD was jealous for his land, and had pity on his people.
b: This passage is a call issued when disaster strikes. God does not judge first; he calls first: “Turn to me with all your heart.” Fasting, weeping, and mourning are not outward forms but true repentance of the heart. Real turning back is not tearing garments for people to see, but tearing the heart for God to see. The problem is not the circumstances; it is the heart.

God’s nature is grace and mercy. He is slow to anger and delights to forgive. Repentance is not a bargaining chip but a return to relationship. When people leave their rightful place and cling to their own way, they fall into chaos; when they humbly turn to God, they are realigned with his heart. Humility is the key to revival.

This also stresses corporate repentance: blowing the trumpet, gathering, and calling a solemn assembly. From elders to children, from bridegroom to bride, all turn to God together. When the priests weep and intercede between the porch and the altar, God becomes jealous for his land and has pity on his people. When God’s people truly return, God himself goes to work.
a: Repent truly
Examine your heart and open it to God, not just going through the motions.
Return to God’s grace
Believe he is glad to forgive, and don’t let shame block your return.
Intercede for the community
Be a watchman in prayer in your family and church.
q: Am I tearing my garments for people to see, or tearing my heart in repentance before God?
pr: Heavenly Father, shine Your light on my hidden heart so that I truly return to You. Forgive my formal religiosity and lead me into deep repentance. Be zealous for Your people, have mercy on us, and bring renewal and revival. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I tear my heart and return to God; he will respond to me with grace and mercy.

t: From Death to Life Is Grace
v: You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins,
in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience.
We also all once lived among them in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest.
But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us,
even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—
and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,
that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus;
for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God,
not of works, that no one would boast.
b: This passage first exposes our former condition: dead in sin, following the world, and pulled along by desires. We were separated from God and powerless to save ourselves. But the turning point is “But God”: God is rich in mercy, and because of his great love he made us alive together with Christ. Salvation is not human striving but God’s grace, freely given.

He not only made us alive, but raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places. This is a change of identity and an elevation of position. From children of wrath to people of grace, from an earthly life into heavenly glory. All of this is a display of grace.

“By grace you have been saved through faith.” Faith is not merit but receiving. It is not of works, so that no one may boast. When we understand this grace, we no longer exalt ourselves, but let Jesus have all the glory.
a: Remember grace
Often recall how God rescued you from death to life.
Live out your new identity
Since you are alive with Christ, no longer follow the old life.
Be humble and thankful
Everything is grace; take no glory for yourself.
q: Am I still trying to prove myself by works, or resting in God’s grace?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You that when I was dead in sin, You made me alive with Christ because of Your great love. Help me always to be thankful and not boast, but to boast only in Your grace. Let me live out a new life that glorifies Your name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am saved by grace through faith; alive with Christ, I give all glory to God.

t: The Blessing of Obedience and God’s Presence
v: “‘If you walk in my statutes and keep my commandments, and do them,
